doc.title: Holly Hofmann interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Jazz audiences and music in schools
summary: They discuss aging audiences at jazz parties, younger festival audiences, and weak school music and arts support in California.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: When I look at some of these festivals, I notice, unfortunately the audience seems to be over 55, and white, and I’m hoping that would change but I don’t know if it will.

I think jazz parties that is the case. That seems to be the demographic that has the money and the interest in going to the jazz parties. The festivals I see are starting to change. Younger people are getting involved in the festivals, there certainly is a wide range of ethnic groups and age groups now, more and more. And of course jazz festivals have had to incorporate some of the younger musicians and also the more contemporary so-called jazz artists, to draw that element in, but I don’t know if it’s such a bad thing. Jazz is presented — there’s a lot of styles of jazz, and things that are called jazz that aren’t really, but somehow getting the young, you know we all look at that. My band looks at that a lot of times, at our audience. And we’re very fortunate because we have a lot of young listeners here in San Diego that come to the Sheraton to hear us play, and we’re thrilled about that, because the music has to be passed down. I sometimes wonder if I’m
going to have enough audience when I’m Moody’s age, you know? When I’m in my 70s, I want somebody to still listen to the music.
How does that happen? Am I correct in hearing that California has very little music in the schools anymore?

I think there’s a lot of states that don’t have a lot of music. California doesn’t have much. I think there are though, in every state, and as I go to a place like IAJE’s convention, I realize there are the individuals and the programs that still have band programs that the kids are learning so much and responding to. And I think it’s just a matter of those individuals that keep those programs going, keeping them going, trying to expand them, until art becomes, the arts become in again. San Diego is not a very — we have lost our symphony for some time, they’ll be going back to work here soon. So I think California needs to work harder at supporting their arts, for sure.
